subject: 거짓말과 침묵의 차이
title: Between saying what is false and saying nothing
content: Most moral traditions condemn lying while permitting a good deal of silence. Somebody who states a falsehood has done something wrong; somebody who declines to mention an inconvenient truth is usually thought to have done nothing at all. Since both may leave the listener equally mistaken, the distinction requires justification rather than mere assertion. One defence appeals to what an assertion does. When I tell you something, I invite you to rely upon my word, and if the word is false I have used that invitation as an instrument against you. Silence issues no such invitation, therefore the listener's error is their own inference rather than my construction. On this reading the moral difference lies in authorship of the false belief. A second defence appeals to what would follow otherwise. If concealing any relevant truth were as wrong as lying, then every conversation would carry an unlimited duty of disclosure, and ordinary life would become impossible. Some reserve is necessary for privacy, for tact, and simply for getting anything done, so a general obligation to volunteer everything cannot be right. Yet the distinction is frequently abused. Silence maintained precisely because it will mislead, in circumstances where the other party reasonably expects to be told, achieves everything a lie achieves while preserving the speaker's ability to claim they never said anything false. Such conduct deserves the same moral verdict as lying, since the intention and the effect are identical. What follows is a more demanding principle than the traditional one. The relevant question is not whether false words were uttered but whether the speaker deliberately produced a false belief in somebody entitled to the truth. Judged by that standard, a great deal of technically accurate speech in advertising, politics, and ordinary business turns out to be dishonest in the fullest sense.

subject: 감사는 의무인가
title: Whether gratitude can be owed
content: When somebody helps us at cost to themselves, we feel we owe them something. Calling that feeling an obligation is natural, and yet gratitude sits awkwardly among moral duties, because a duty performed grudgingly still counts as performed while gratitude offered grudgingly seems not to count at all. Examining the tension reveals something about which moral demands can be enforced. Part of the difficulty is that gratitude has two components. There is an attitude, involving recognition of what was done and of the giver's good will, and there is an expression, which may be words, reciprocation, or simply readiness to help in turn. The expression can be demanded; the attitude cannot, since attitudes are not produced on request. Therefore any obligation must be stated carefully. A second difficulty concerns what the benefactor may claim. Somebody who helps in order to place another under obligation has not really given, and their subsequent complaint that they were not thanked reveals the transaction they intended. Genuine gifts create no debt of that kind, which is exactly why gratitude cannot be collected like a payment. The moral relation is spoiled by being enforced. What can be defended is a duty of acknowledgement. Failing to recognise what somebody did treats them as though their effort were a natural event rather than a choice, and that failure is a genuine wrong against them. It denies the giver the standing of an agent whose good will mattered. On this reading gratitude belongs to the family of moral responses that includes apology and forgiveness. Each involves recognising the other person as somebody who acted, each loses its value when compelled, and each is nonetheless expected in a way that makes its absence a real fault rather than merely a disappointment.

subject: 규칙을 어길 때의 근거
title: What justifies departing from a rule
content: Rules are useful precisely because they are followed without fresh calculation each time. A rule that yielded whenever somebody judged the outcome better would supply none of the coordination and predictability that made it valuable. Yet nobody believes rules should be followed in every conceivable case, so the moral question is what counts as adequate reason to depart. One answer says that a rule may be broken whenever doing so produces a better result. This collapses the rule into a general instruction to do whatever seems best, and it destroys the very benefit rules provide, since others can no longer predict conduct. Worse, the judgment that this case is exceptional is made by the person who wants the exception, which is not a reliable procedure. A second answer permits departure only where following the rule would defeat its own purpose. A traffic rule exists for safety, therefore a case where obeying it would cause an accident is not really a counterexample but an application of what the rule was for. This test is disciplined, because it requires identifying the purpose and showing that the particular case defeats it, which is a public argument rather than a private preference. A third consideration concerns the cost of a wrong judgment. Where breaking a rule is easily reversible and the stakes are modest, exercising judgment is reasonable. Where the rule guards against catastrophe, or where many people making similar judgments would produce disaster, the case for rigid adherence strengthens considerably. What the argument establishes is that neither strict rule following nor case by case calculation is defensible on its own. Justice requires rules because judgment is unreliable, and it requires judgment because rules are general, and the honest position holds both truths rather than choosing whichever is convenient.

subject: 증언과 신빙성의 배분
title: Who gets believed, and what that costs
content: Most of what anybody knows was learned from somebody else. Since we cannot verify more than a fraction of it, believing testimony is not an occasional shortcut but the ordinary route to knowledge. This makes the distribution of credibility a moral matter as well as an epistemic one. The difficulty is that credibility is not distributed evenly. Speakers are assessed partly on evidence and partly on assumptions attached to their accent, appearance, or position, and those assumptions frequently have nothing to do with reliability. When somebody's testimony is discounted for such reasons, they suffer a distinctive wrong: they are not merely disbelieved but treated as less capable of contributing knowledge, which denies them a standing that belongs to every competent person. The harm compounds. A speaker repeatedly disbelieved may stop offering what they know, and the community loses information it needed. Where whole groups are treated this way, the shared stock of knowledge develops gaps precisely where their experience would have filled them, and those gaps are invisible to everyone whose testimony was accepted. Injustice of this kind therefore damages the pursuit of truth rather than merely the individuals slighted. The remedy is harder than it appears. Simply resolving to believe everybody equally is unworkable, since assessing reliability is a legitimate and necessary part of using testimony. What is required instead is attention to which of our assessments track evidence and which track prejudice, and that distinction is difficult because both feel identical from inside. What can be recommended is a form of intellectual humility. When somebody's account strikes us as implausible, the possibility that our sense of plausibility was formed by a narrow experience deserves genuine consideration, and treating that possibility seriously is among the more demanding moral requirements of ordinary conversation.

subject: 미래의 나에 대한 의무
title: What you owe the person you will become
content: A decision taken today binds somebody who cannot object: the person you will be in twenty years. That person will inherit your habits, your health, and your commitments without having chosen any of them, which raises a genuine moral question about whether obligations run forward through a single life. The question seems strange because we ordinarily treat prudence as self interest rather than as duty. Yet the relation between present and future self resembles the relation between distinct persons in several respects. Their values may differ, their interests certainly do, and the earlier one holds nearly all the power. Where one party can bind another who has no voice, moral language is usually appropriate. One position pushes the analogy hard, arguing that harming your future self is wrong in the way harming anybody is wrong. This has the merit of explaining why we criticise reckless conduct even where nobody else is affected. It strains, however, against the fact that the future person will remember these decisions as their own, which no genuine third party ever does. A more moderate position keeps the moral vocabulary while acknowledging the continuity. What you owe the future self is not the respect owed a stranger but something like fidelity to a shared project, since the two of you are engaged in one life. On this reading recklessness is a failure of care toward a person whose fate is bound to yours rather than a wrong against an outsider. The practical value of the framing lies in what it corrects. Treating prudence as mere preference makes it seem optional, whereas most people regret failures of foresight in a way that resembles guilt rather than disappointment. That resemblance suggests our ordinary moral thinking already recognises a duty here, even where our theories do not.

subject: 몸에 대한 권리
title: The claim a person has over their own body
content: Among the least disputed moral claims is that a person may determine what happens to their own body. Medical treatment requires consent, unwanted touching is a wrong regardless of consequences, and forcing somebody to undergo a procedure for another's benefit is prohibited even where the benefit is enormous. Understanding why this claim carries such weight is worth the effort, because its boundaries are genuinely contested. One justification treats bodily control as the foundation of every other freedom. Whatever else a person may do requires a body to do it with, therefore losing authority over that body means losing authority over everything. On this reading the right is not one liberty among many but the condition of the rest. A second justification appeals to what violation does. Being used without agreement treats a person as a resource rather than as somebody with purposes of their own, and the intimacy of the body makes this particularly plain. The wrong lies in the relation established rather than in any injury inflicted, which explains why harmless violations remain serious. The strength of the claim generates its hardest cases. Nobody may be compelled to donate an organ even to save a life, and defending that conclusion requires accepting a real cost. Some argue the right should yield where the burden is trivial and the benefit immense; others hold that admitting exceptions would make bodily authority conditional on public judgments about worthwhile uses, which destroys what the right protects. What the argument reveals is that this claim differs from most rights in resisting the ordinary weighing of interests. A right that yields whenever the aggregate favours yielding is not a right at all, and the discomfort produced by the hard cases is the price of having one that works.

subject: 자선과 정의의 경계
title: Whether helping is generosity or justice
content: When somebody in need is helped, the act may be described in two very different ways. It may be generosity, freely given and creditable to the giver, or it may be justice, discharging something already owed. The choice between these descriptions changes everything about the moral relation, and disputes about poverty and aid frequently turn on which applies. The difference shows in what follows from failure. If assistance is generosity, refusing it is disappointing but not wrongful, and the recipient has no complaint. If it is justice, refusing wrongs them, and they may demand rather than request. Consequently the description also determines who stands where: charity places the giver above the recipient, while justice places them as equals with one owing the other. Which description fits depends on how the need arose. Where somebody's poverty results from arrangements that benefited others — rules about property, work, or exchange that some helped establish and from which they gained — the resulting claim looks like justice rather than generosity. Where the need arose from misfortune nobody arranged, the case for a duty of assistance rests on different ground, and calling it charity is more defensible. This matters for how institutions are designed. Assistance framed as generosity depends on the willingness of givers, invites gratitude as its price, and can be withdrawn. Assistance framed as justice is claimable, predictable, and does not require the recipient to perform deference. Anyone who has needed help understands that the difference is not merely verbal. What follows is that the argument about welfare is rarely about compassion at all. It is an argument about whether existing arrangements produced the need, and answering that question honestly determines whether what is owed is kindness or something considerably more demanding.

subject: 문화 상대주의의 한계
title: How far difference can excuse a practice
content: Moral practices differ enormously between societies, and the observation has led some to conclude that no standard exists beyond each culture's own. On this view criticising another society's practices merely applies local prejudice at a distance, and the appropriate response to difference is tolerance rather than judgment. The position has genuine appeal. It reflects a proper humility about our own certainties, many of which our ancestors held with equal confidence and we now reject. It also responds to a real history in which moral criticism served as an instrument of conquest, so suspicion of confident judgment is not merely fashionable. Yet the position collapses under examination. If each culture's standards were final, then reformers within a society would always be wrong, since they oppose the prevailing view by definition. Every moral advance would become a moral corruption at the moment it began, and that conclusion should be rejected because it makes progress unintelligible. Moreover the doctrine cannot state itself consistently, since tolerance is offered as a value binding on everyone while denying that any value binds everyone. A more defensible position separates two claims. That our confidence should be tempered by awareness of our own limits is true and important. That no argument can ever cross a cultural boundary is false, as demonstrated by the fact that such arguments regularly succeed. People do change their minds when shown that a practice rests on a factual error or contradicts something they already hold. What survives is a working rule. Difference is a reason for careful inquiry before judging, since practices frequently make sense in contexts outsiders misunderstand. It is not a reason for permanent silence, particularly when those most harmed by a practice are themselves objecting and asking to be heard.

subject: 감시가 바꾸는 행동
title: How being watched alters what people do
content: Observation changes conduct. People behave differently when they believe somebody is watching, and this effect appears even where the observer has no power to punish. The moral significance of this fact is frequently overlooked in arguments about surveillance, which tend to focus on what watchers might do with the information rather than on what watching itself accomplishes. The change is not always for the worse. Knowing that conduct is visible restrains some genuinely harmful behaviour, and institutions have always relied on that fact. Yet the effect is indiscriminate, since observation restrains conduct according to whether it would be criticised rather than whether it is wrong. Under sustained watching people converge on whatever is currently approved, and that convergence is a loss even where everything approved happens to be good. What is lost is the space in which somebody may try a position, hold an unpopular view, or behave oddly without accounting for it. Moral progress has depended repeatedly on people who did exactly these things, therefore a society that eliminates the space also eliminates the mechanism by which its own errors get corrected. This argument does not require any misuse of the information collected. A second consideration concerns the relation established. Being watched by somebody who is not watched in return places a person in a position they did not choose, and the asymmetry persists whether or not anything is done with what is seen. Justice between parties of unequal power depends on limiting exactly such asymmetries. What follows is that the familiar defence — that innocent people have nothing to fear — misses the point entirely. The harm of comprehensive observation falls on the guilty and the innocent alike, because it operates by changing what everybody is willing to do rather than by catching anyone.

subject: 창작자와 작품의 분리
title: Whether a work survives what its maker did
content: When somebody who made admired work turns out to have behaved terribly, audiences face a genuine moral question. Should the work now be avoided, and if so on what ground? The question is asked frequently and answered badly, usually by asserting one of two extreme positions without argument. The first position holds that the work is entirely independent. What was made stands on its own, its value lies in its properties rather than in its maker's conduct, and refusing it punishes nobody while depriving the audience. This has real force, particularly for work whose content bears no relation to the wrongdoing. The second position holds that engaging with the work supports the person. Attention and money flow to them, their reputation is sustained, and the audience becomes a participant in something they would otherwise condemn. This too has force, although it applies unevenly, since it says little about a maker who is long dead. Careful thinking separates several distinct questions that the debate usually merges. Whether the work is good is one question, whether engaging with it benefits the wrongdoer is another, and whether the wrongdoing shows in the work itself is a third. These may receive different answers, and treating them as one produces the confident nonsense that fills such arguments. The third question is the most interesting. Sometimes the conduct and the work are unrelated, and knowing about the first tells us nothing about the second. Sometimes the work displays the very attitudes that produced the conduct, in which case the knowledge genuinely changes what a careful reader sees, and refusing the work is a judgment about the work rather than about its maker. Distinguishing these cases requires attention rather than a general policy, which is why no rule settles the matter in advance.

subject: 동물의 지위
title: What we owe to creatures who cannot argue
content: Animals cannot state claims, enter agreements, or participate in the practices through which moral obligations are usually negotiated. Some philosophers have concluded from this that they fall outside morality entirely, and that our treatment of them is a matter of taste rather than of justice. The conclusion is worth examining, because the argument supporting it proves too much. If moral standing required the capacity to argue, then infants and those with severe cognitive impairment would also lack it, and almost nobody accepts that result. Therefore the capacity to participate cannot be the criterion, and a different account is needed for both cases. The obvious candidate is the capacity to be affected: a creature that can suffer has something at stake, and that fact alone gives others reason to consider it. Accepting this does not settle how much weight such interests carry. Most people hold that a human life matters more than an animal's, and defending that judgment requires identifying a morally relevant difference. Candidates include the capacity to plan, to hold relationships across time, and to have a life that can go well or badly in a fuller sense. These are genuine differences, although they justify weighing interests differently rather than ignoring them altogether. What the argument rules out is the position that animal suffering counts for nothing. Once it is granted that suffering matters where it occurs, the burden falls on anyone who inflicts it to show that the purpose is worth the cost. Many practices cannot meet that burden, since the interest served is convenience or preference while the cost is considerable. The practical conclusion is therefore uncomfortable rather than extreme. It does not require treating animals as equals; it requires giving reasons, and a great many current practices have never been asked for any.

subject: 미노아 궁전의 저장실
title: What the storerooms of a palace reveal
content: The great buildings of ancient Crete are called palaces, although the label may mislead. Their most striking feature is not a throne room but row upon row of narrow storage chambers, lined with enormous jars and connected by corridors that occupy an extraordinary share of the total floor area. Any account of this civilization must explain why so much of its architecture was devoted to keeping things. The jars held oil, grain, and wine, and their capacity was very large. Estimates from one site suggest storage sufficient to feed a substantial population for a considerable period, therefore the building was functioning as a centre of collection and distribution rather than merely as a residence. Clay tablets recovered nearby record quantities received and issued, which supports the same reading. This suggests an economy organised around the centre. Producers delivered a share of their harvest, the palace stored and redistributed it, and specialists working within the complex were supported from those stores. Such an arrangement appears in several ancient civilizations of the region, and it explains features that would otherwise be puzzling, including the scale of the workshops and the elaborate accounting. The system also explains a vulnerability. A centre holding the surplus of a whole territory concentrates risk, since damage to the complex removes the reserve that many households depended upon. Several of these buildings were destroyed and rebuilt more than once during the era, and the final destructions were not followed by reconstruction. What archaeology supplies here is a structure rather than a story. We can measure the jars, read the quantities, and map the corridors, yet the tablets record only accounts, so the names and intentions of those who directed this civilization remain almost entirely unknown to us.

subject: 욕구 충족과 웰빙
title: Whether getting what you want makes life go well
content: One influential account holds that a life goes well to the extent that a person's desires are satisfied. The theory is attractive because it avoids imposing anybody's standards on anybody else, treating each person as the authority on what counts as their own good. Whatever they want is what makes their life better, and no external judgment intrudes. The difficulty appears when we examine which desires should count. People want things based on false beliefs, and satisfying such a desire frequently makes their life worse rather than better. Somebody who wants a particular medicine because they think it will cure them gains nothing when it does not, therefore the theory must exclude desires resting on error. That exclusion is reasonable, although it concedes that the person's actual wanting is not decisive. A second difficulty concerns desires about matters remote from the person's life. If I want a stranger I will never meet to recover from illness, and they do recover without my ever learning of it, my desire has been satisfied, and yet nothing about my life seems to have improved. This suggests the theory needs a further restriction to desires about one's own life, which again narrows the authority it granted. A third difficulty concerns adaptation. People frequently adjust their wants downward when their circumstances are constrained, and somebody who has learned to want very little may report full satisfaction while living under conditions that justice would condemn. Counting that as a life going well seems plainly wrong, and the theory has no obvious resource for saying so. What survives is a modified view in which informed desires about one's own life carry considerable weight without being the whole measure. That position is more defensible and less tidy, which is frequently the shape of the truth in moral philosophy.

subject: 스키타이 기마 문화의 무덤
title: Frozen tombs of the mounted nomads
content: The Scythians left no cities and almost no writing, and for a long time everything known about this ancient people came from Greek authors who found them alarming. Then archaeologists began to open their burial mounds, and what came out of the ground changed the picture entirely. In the high valleys of central Asia, water seeped into some of these ancient tombs and froze there for good. The ice held cloth, wood, leather, and even human skin across more than two thousand years. So archaeologists lifted rugs, saddles, coats, and tattooed bodies out of an era that elsewhere leaves only metal and pots, and the finds showed a way of life far richer than the written accounts had allowed. The graves describe a civilization built around the horse. Animals were buried beside their riders, still in harness and still decked out, sometimes in large numbers. Weapons, cups, and gold work lie with the dead, and the same animal designs turn up across an enormous stretch of ground, which shows shared custom among groups spread from the Black Sea to the edge of China. Several graves of this era held women buried with weapons. That finding cuts both ways, since it suggests the ancient authors were reporting rather than inventing, while also reminding us that they wrote down whatever struck them as odd. What the mounds prove is that a people can move constantly and still build something complex. This civilization had no towns, and yet it fed skilled metalworkers, drew goods across huge distances, and held one style of art steady for centuries. Our habit of giving history to those who built in stone reflects what survives rather than what was achieved, and these frozen graves correct that bias more sharply than any argument could.

subject: 의도와 예견의 구분
title: Between what you aim at and what you expect
content: A distinction that appears constantly in moral argument separates what somebody intends from what they merely foresee. A surgeon who administers pain relief expecting it may shorten a life is judged differently from one who administers a drug in order to end that life, although the outcome may be identical. Whether this distinction can bear the weight placed upon it is genuinely disputed. The case for it rests on what intention reveals. Somebody who aims at a harm has made it part of their plan, so that if the harm failed to occur they would count their action unsuccessful. Somebody who merely foresees it would be relieved if it did not occur, since it forms no part of what they set out to achieve. This difference in the structure of the agent's plan seems morally significant, because it shows what they were prepared to use as a means. The case against points at the outcome. The person harmed suffers identically whichever description applies, and telling them that their injury was foreseen rather than intended offers little. Critics add that the distinction is easy to manipulate, since a sufficiently ingenious agent can redescribe almost any intention as a side effect of some more acceptable aim. Both observations have force. A moderate position preserves the distinction while denying that it settles anything by itself. Foreseeing a serious harm requires justification, and the fact that it was not aimed at does not remove the burden. What the distinction does is mark a difference in how the agent treated the person harmed, and treating somebody as a means deserves a heavier verdict than harming them incidentally. That is a genuine moral difference, although it is one consideration among several rather than a formula for deciding hard cases.

subject: 하지 않음과 함의 차이
title: Whether letting happen is the same as doing
content: Our moral judgments treat causing a harm as considerably worse than failing to prevent one. Pushing somebody into a river is murder; declining to pull them out is, in most legal systems, no offence at all. Whether this asymmetry reflects a genuine moral difference or merely a convenient habit is among the most argued questions in ethics. The case against the distinction is straightforward. In both scenarios somebody dies who could have lived, the agent could have altered the outcome, and the agent's reasons may be identical. If the death is equally bad and equally avoidable, singling out one case for condemnation appears arbitrary, and defenders of this view conclude that our failure to prevent distant suffering is far worse than we admit. The case for the distinction appeals to what a moral requirement demands. A duty not to kill can be satisfied by everybody simultaneously without limiting anybody's plans, whereas a duty to prevent every preventable death would consume every life entirely, since preventable deaths are always occurring. Therefore the asymmetry may reflect the practical structure of obligations rather than mere prejudice about outcomes. A second consideration concerns the relation between agent and victim. Somebody who kills has intervened in another's life and redirected it; somebody who fails to help has left a situation as they found it. Even where the outcome is equally bad, the moral relation differs, and justice attends to relations as well as to results. What most careful positions conclude is that the distinction is real but weaker than ordinary judgment assumes. Failing to prevent a serious harm at trivial cost is not innocent, even where it is not killing, and the comfortable belief that only actions require justification does not survive examination.

subject: 앙코르의 저수 체계
title: The reservoirs that carried a medieval capital
content: The temples of Angkor draw every visitor, and yet the largest works at this ancient site are not buildings but reservoirs. Huge rectangular basins, banked up above the plain, run for kilometres, and a web of channels ties them to the rivers and to the fields. Any account of this medieval civilization has to explain why so much labour went into holding water. The climate of the region makes the reason perfectly plain. Rain arrives in one short season and then nearly stops, and therefore a people living on rice faced abundance followed by scarcity every year. Holding the surplus and letting it out through the dry months turns an impossible pattern into a workable one, and the sheer size of the basins points to a very large population. Whether these works mainly served the fields was argued about for several decades. Some scholars stressed religious meaning, reading the basins as a great ocean around a sacred mountain, and noting that the inscriptions of the era say little about farming. Others pointed instead at the channels running toward the cultivated ground. Survey from the air, using radar that sees through the canopy, has largely settled it by exposing a wide grid of canals, banks, and field walls far beyond the temples. However, that same survey also exposed a serious weakness. A system of such size needs constant maintenance, because silt builds up in the channels and has to be removed again and again. Although the network held for centuries, signs of hasty repair, broken banks, and abandoned stretches appear in the later centuries of the kingdom, and tree rings from the same period record violent swings between drought and flood. What emerges is a civilization whose greatest work was also its greatest exposure. The channels fed a population that could not have lived there without them, and when the channels failed, that crowding could no longer be held together.

subject: 다수를 위한 소수의 희생
title: When numbers are not enough
content: Suppose a harm falling on one person would prevent a greater harm falling on many. The arithmetic seems to settle the matter, and yet moral judgment frequently refuses the conclusion, particularly where the one person must be used rather than merely affected. Understanding that refusal is central to the argument between competing moral theories. One tradition treats the arithmetic as decisive. What matters is how much suffering occurs, and where fewer suffer the outcome is better, so any arrangement producing that result is justified. The position has real strength, since denying it appears to prefer a worse outcome for the sake of keeping one's own conduct clean. The opposing tradition holds that persons are not quantities to be summed. Each individual has a claim not to be used as an instrument for others' benefit, and that claim is not outweighed by adding up gains distributed among strangers. On this view the person sacrificed is not merely a smaller number on the losing side; they are somebody to whom the arrangement cannot be justified. The distinction between harming somebody as a means and harming them as a side effect does considerable work here. Diverting a danger so that fewer are struck is different from using a person's body to stop it, although the totals may match, and most people's judgments track that difference reliably across many variations of the case. Whether the judgments reflect a moral truth or a psychological quirk is precisely what is disputed. What both sides accept is that the numbers matter somewhat. The disagreement concerns whether they matter absolutely, and the practical stakes are considerable, since institutions making decisions about safety, medicine, and public risk must adopt some position, usually without ever stating which one they have chosen.

subject: 고구려 벽화 무덤의 인물
title: Painted tombs of a northern kingdom
content: The kingdom of Goguryeo held a wide territory across the northern part of the Korean peninsula and beyond for some seven centuries. Its written records are scarce, since the histories that survive were composed by others or long afterwards, and much of what can be said about daily life in this ancient state comes from painted tombs. Several dozen chambered burials carry murals on their plastered walls. The earliest concentrate on the occupants, showing a seated figure receiving attendants, alongside scenes of kitchens, stables, and processions. Because the painters recorded what surrounded them rather than what a chronicle would preserve, these images supply detail no text provides: the cut of clothing, the shape of vessels, the arrangement of a household, and the equipment of a rider. One celebrated tomb displays a hunting scene across an entire wall. Mounted archers pursue deer and tiger, twisting backward in the saddle to shoot, and the horses are drawn with a sense of movement that is unusual for the era. Such images tell us what the elite of this civilization valued, and they connect the kingdom to a wider world, since the same hunting motif appears across the steppe and into central Asia. Later tombs shift toward mythological subjects, with guardian creatures occupying the four walls according to a scheme shared across the region. That change indicates altered beliefs about the afterlife rather than altered painting technique, and dating the shift helps historians trace the movement of religious ideas into the peninsula. Preservation is now the pressing problem. Many chambers were opened long ago, and exposure to changed air has damaged pigments that survived for a millennium and a half underground. What these paintings offer is a rare direct view of an ancient society, and much of it is fading faster than it is being recorded.

subject: 원칙과 판단력
title: Why principles never decide a case by themselves
content: Moral education tends to concentrate on principles: do not lie, keep your promises, prevent harm where you can. Learning them is genuinely valuable, and yet anybody who has faced a difficult situation knows that the principles rarely announce which of them applies or what they require here. The gap between holding a principle and knowing what to do is where most of the difficulty lives. Part of the gap concerns identification. Before a rule about promises applies, somebody must recognise that what occurred was a promise rather than a prediction or a hope, and that recognition is not itself supplied by the rule. Every principle presupposes a description of the situation, and choosing the right description is frequently the whole of the problem. Part of the gap concerns conflict. Principles collide regularly, and no principle explains which yields, since a rule ranking them would face the same difficulty at the next level. Somebody must weigh, and weighing is a capacity rather than a procedure. This is why two people who share every stated principle may disagree entirely about a case without either having made a logical mistake. What fills the gap is judgment, and judgment is acquired the way practical skills generally are: through experience, attention to particular cases, and correction by people who have more of it. This explains why moral wisdom is not distributed according to how many principles somebody can recite, and why those who reason best about difficult situations frequently articulate their reasons poorly. The conclusion is not that principles are useless. They organise attention, they resist self serving improvisation, and they make it possible to explain a decision to somebody else. What they cannot do is remove the need for the very capacity that makes their application possible, and pretending otherwise produces reasoning that is confident and wrong.

subject: 사과가 하는 일
title: What an apology accomplishes
content: An apology changes something, although it is difficult to say what. The harm remains, the past is unaltered, and the words themselves supply no compensation. Yet an offered apology frequently repairs a relation that money could not, and a withheld apology can keep a grievance alive for decades. Understanding the mechanism reveals something about how moral relations work. An apology performs several distinct things at once. It acknowledges that a wrong occurred, which contradicts any suggestion that the injured party misunderstood or overreacted. It accepts that the speaker was responsible rather than unlucky. And it expresses regret, which signals that the speaker holds the same moral view of the act as the person harmed. Each element does separate work, and an apology missing one of them is felt to be incomplete. This explains why certain formulations fail so conspicuously. Expressing regret that somebody felt hurt acknowledges an emotional state without conceding that a wrong occurred, and it therefore performs the appearance of the first element while actually denying it. Listeners detect the substitution reliably, and the attempt usually leaves the relation worse than silence would have. The deepest function concerns standing. A wrong treats the victim as somebody whose interests could be disregarded, and an apology withdraws that message, restoring them to the position of somebody whose treatment mattered. This is why the words can matter even where nothing practical follows, and why they are demanded long after any material remedy has become impossible. The limits follow from the same account. An apology cannot be owed by somebody who did nothing, cannot be extracted without losing its meaning, and cannot substitute for repair where repair is possible. What it offers is a correction of the moral record, which is a real thing to offer and not a substitute for anything else.

subject: 마오리 요새 유적의 구조
title: Terraced hills of a Pacific people
content: Across the landscape of New Zealand, hundreds of hills carry terraces, ditches, and banks cut by hand. These are the remains of fortified settlements built by Maori communities, and they represent one of the largest programmes of earthwork construction undertaken by any people without metal tools. Their distribution and their design tell a good deal about the history of the islands. The settlements were established from the fourteenth century onward, after several generations of expansion following the original Polynesian arrival. Their appearance coincides with rising population, the spread of cultivated ground, and increasing competition for the best land, therefore archaeologists read them as evidence of a change in how communities related to one another rather than as a practice brought from elsewhere. The engineering is careful. Steep natural slopes were scarped to make them unclimbable, ditches were cut across the accessible approaches, and the excavated soil was thrown up as banks topped with timber palisades. Entrances were narrow and overlooked, so an attacker had to advance through a confined space under fire from above. Within the defences, terraces provided level ground for houses and for storage pits holding the sweet potato crop through winter. Those pits point to the underlying purpose. A community that stores food creates something worth taking, and the same store that carried it through the cold season made it a target. Consequently the defences protected not only people but the surplus on which their survival depended, which is a pattern found in many agricultural societies across history. What survives now is largely the shape of the ground, since the timber has long gone. Walking these terraces one reads a landscape of decisions about where to live, what to defend, and whom to fear, recorded in earth rather than in writing.

subject: 자기 기만은 어떻게 가능한가
title: How a person deceives themselves
content: Deceiving somebody else is straightforward: I know the truth and lead you to believe otherwise. Deceiving oneself appears to require holding both roles simultaneously, knowing the truth while successfully believing its opposite, and stated that way the phenomenon looks impossible. Yet everybody recognises it, which means the description must be wrong somewhere. One resolution denies that full knowledge is present. What the self deceiver has is not settled knowledge but evidence, and evidence can be handled selectively. They attend to whatever supports the comfortable conclusion, examine contrary material with unusual severity, and stop investigating at the convenient moment. No contradictory beliefs are held at once, therefore the puzzle dissolves into a description of biased inquiry. A second resolution points to what the person does rather than what they believe. Somebody avoiding a diagnosis does not decide to believe they are well; they simply do not make the appointment. The false belief is maintained by arranging never to test it, which requires no logical impossibility and considerable practical effort. This explains why self deception is so frequently visible to others: the avoidance is conspicuous even where the belief is not. What makes the phenomenon a moral matter rather than merely a psychological curiosity is that it is motivated. The person is not making a random error; they are protecting something, usually a picture of themselves they cannot afford to revise. Consequently self deception tends to cluster precisely around one's own conduct, where the truth would demand a change. The practical implication is uncomfortable. Since the mechanism operates by preventing inquiry, introspection is a poor detector, and somebody deceiving themselves feels exactly like somebody who is right. The available remedies are external: seeking the judgment of people willing to disagree, and treating one's own reluctance to examine a question as evidence rather than as preference.

subject: 테오티우아칸 도시의 규모
title: A city whose rulers left no portraits
content: At its height, more than fifteen centuries ago, Teotihuacan held perhaps a hundred thousand people, which made it among the largest cities anywhere at the time. It was laid out on a rigid grid oriented to a single axis, dominated by two enormous pyramids and a broad avenue running for kilometres. Every account of ancient civilization in the Americas must reckon with its scale. What distinguishes the city is not the monuments but the housing. Excavation has revealed hundreds of walled residential compounds, each accommodating perhaps sixty to a hundred people in apartments arranged around courtyards. The compounds were substantially built, plastered, and frequently painted with murals, which indicates a general standard of living unusual for the era rather than luxury confined to an elite. Occupants of different compounds appear to have specialised in different crafts. Equally striking is what the city does not display. Other civilizations of the region covered their monuments with images of named rulers and their conquests. Here almost no such portraits appear, and the murals show masked figures, deities, and processions rather than individuals. Whether power rested with a council, with competing houses, or with a monarchy that simply avoided personal display remains genuinely unresolved after a century of excavation. Analysis of remains shows that people came from considerable distances, with distinct districts occupied by groups whose pottery and burial customs match regions far to the south and east. The city therefore drew population across a wide territory, which suggests it offered something worth travelling for. Its end came with burning concentrated on the ceremonial centre rather than on the residential districts, which points to internal upheaval rather than to conquest from outside. The city emptied gradually afterwards, and the ruins remained impressive enough that later peoples treated the site as sacred ground.
